column3: Walk right, punch everything. Side-scrolling brawlers built for two players on one panel: grab a friend, share the turkey, clear the stage.
One-on-one versus games, the reason this cabinet has six buttons. Top row punches, bottom row kicks, and every quarter-circle motion lands on a real stick.
Single-screen chase games from the golden age. Learn the patterns, clear the board, push your score one more level.
Run, jump, and time it right. Tight d-pad action that plays even better on an arcade stick.
Falling blocks, matching gems, and chain reactions. Quick to learn, hard to put down, and brutal head-to-head.
Racers that steer fine on a digital stick: top-down mayhem, arcade sprint, and no analog wheel required.
Never stop shooting. Side-scrolling action where you move and fire at the same time, best with a second player.
Shoot 'em ups: vertical and horizontal shooters, from the 8-bit classics to Cave's bullet curtains. Learn the patterns, hunt the high score.
Arcade sports with big moves and short rules: two-on-two dunks, flying discs, and anything you can settle in one credit.
One player, two sticks: Player 1 stick moves, Player 2 stick aims and fires. Each game has its own control setup.
Games for a crowd: quick rounds, simple controls, lots of shouting.
Games with a RetroAchievements set, matched to your own ROMs. The first line of each game shows how many you have unlocked, and whether in hardcore.
The golden age: single-screen classics, pattern play, and three lives for a quarter.
Scrolling stages, power-ups, and the first big sprites: the arcade grows up and the home consoles catch on.
The peak: one-on-one fighters change everything, 16-bit consoles battle, and every arcade has a row of fighters.
Polygons arrive, 2D gets its most beautiful sprites, and the CD consoles take over the living room.
The last great arcade era: Dreamcast, NAOMI, Cave's bullet hell, and the final 2D masterpieces.
A 1988 arcade board: side-scrolling brawlers, the first big one-on-one fighters, and an era-defining library.
The 1993 successor board: fighters, versus crossovers, and some of the best beat 'em ups ever made.
The last board of the line: 2D fighters and some of the finest sprite work ever made.
Sega's final console (1998), arcade-perfect for its time: versus fighters, Soulcalibur, Ikaruga, and the NAOMI ports.
The wider arcade library through FinalBurn Neo: Konami, Taito, Irem, Toaplan, Cave, Data East, and more.
Sega's 16-bit console (1988): blast processing, Streets of Rage, Gunstar Heroes, and a mean six-button pad.
Nintendo's 1996 console, picked for the games that play well without an analog stick.
SNK's arcade-and-home system (1990): King of Fighters, Metal Slug, Samurai Shodown, and a four-button layout.
Nintendo's 8-bit console (1983): the platformers, shooters, and action games that started it all.
NEC's little powerhouse (1987), also known as the TurboGrafx-16: the shooter console, with CD-ROM extras.
Sony's first PlayStation (1994): the 2D fighters and shooters that ignore the analog sticks.
Sega's 1994 console, a 2D monster: arcade-perfect fighters and shooters that never left Japan.
The Genesis CD add-on (1991): CD soundtracks, bigger games, and Sonic CD.
Nintendo's 16-bit console (1990): arcade fighter ports, Contra III, and the platformers everyone remembers.
Where it all began: Space Invaders, Asteroids, Galaxian, and the first home consoles. One stick, one button, one more try.
Atari's 1977 console that put arcade games in the living room: one stick, one button, and Space Invaders, Pitfall!, River Raid and Yars' Revenge.
The blue bomber: run, jump, shoot, and steal the boss's weapon, from the NES originals to the X series.
The Toaplan shooters, the studio that wrote the book on vertical shmups before Cave took over: Tiger-Heli, Twin Cobra, Truxton, Batsugun.
Cave's bullet curtains: Mushihime-Sama, Espgaluda, Ketsui, Deathsmiles and the other manic shooters.
SNK's team-based crossover fighter, one chapter per year from '94 to 2003, played on the Neo Geo four-button layout.
Konami's shooter family: Gradius and its power-up bar, Salamander and Life Force, and the Parodius spoofs.
SNK's duelling fighter series, from Terry Bogard's first tournament to Garou: Mark of the Wolves.
Place bombs, trap your friends, and try to stay out of the blast: Hudson's maze-battle series.
Konami's turtles in the arcade brawler, the SNES sequel, and the fighting games that followed.
The original street brawler and its sequels: Technos Japan's fists, elbows, and two-player punch-ups.
Falling blocks in every flavour: the arcade original, the Grand Master version, and the N64 spin-offs.
Westone's platform and action-adventure family, from the arcade Wonder Boy to Monster World.
The vertical shooter line: 1941, 1942, 1943, 1944 and 19XX, one plane and a lot of bullets.
Konami's whip-and-torch vampire hunt, from the NES trilogy to Super Castlevania IV.
Konami's run and gun: two commandos, one spread gun, and no time to reload.
Psikyo's Strikers 1945 and Video System's Aero Fighters: warplane shooters with big personality.
Cave's founding shooter and its sequels: DonPachi, DoDonPachi and the later Dai-Fukkatsu and SaiDaiOuJou versions.
The ape that started Nintendo's arcade era, and the Rareware sequels on the SNES.
Falling-blob and bubble-popping puzzle games, best head to head: Puyo Puyo, Puzzle Bobble and Mean Bean Machine.
Irem's horizontal shooter with the charge beam and the detachable Force pod.
Namco's alien-swarm shooters: Galaga and its sequels, plus Galaxian and Gaplus.
The yellow maze-muncher and his friends, from Pac-Man to Ms. Pac-Man and Pac-Land.
Sega's ninja action series, from the arcade original to The Revenge of Shinobi and Shinobi III.
Sega's blue hedgehog, from Genesis speed runs to the arcade SegaSonic.
SNK's hand-drawn run and gun on the Neo Geo: tanks, prisoners to rescue, and enormous explosions.
SNK's weapon-based fighting series: slow, deadly, and one clean hit can end a round.
Brutal armoured-knight platformers: Ghosts'n Goblins, Ghouls'n Ghosts and Super Ghouls'n Ghosts.
Tecmo's ninja action games, from the arcade brawler to the NES trilogy.
Taito's bubble-blowing dragons and their rainbow-making cousins, with a two-player mode made for the cabinet.
Sega's sword-and-sorcery brawler series: pick a hero and fight your way to Death Adder.
Nintendo's plumber outside the NES: Mario Bros. in the arcade, plus Mario Kart and Super Mario World on the SNES.
Midway's blood-soaked fighting series, with the digitised fighters and fatalities that caused a stir.
Hudson's scrolling shooter series for the PC Engine: Soldier Blade, Super Star Soldier and Fantasy Star Soldier.
SNK's fighting series with the zooming camera and spirit gauge, from the first game to the Path of the Warrior.
Sega's Genesis beat 'em up trilogy, famous for its soundtrack and its two-player brawling.
Marvel fighters and brawlers, from Children of the Atom to the versus crossovers, plus Konami's X-Men and The Punisher.
Namco's horror brawler: Rick, the Terror Mask, and a mansion full of things to hit with a two-by-four.
Dig holes, trap the guards and grab the gold: Irem's arcade Lode Runners and Psikyo's head-to-head Dig Fight.
Taito's 1978 alien march that started it all, plus the DX and '95 remakes.
Atari's vector cockpit run on the Death Star, plus the Super Star Wars games on the SNES.
Technosoft's shooter series: pick your weapon, keep it, and fly through Thunder Force III and Lightening Force.
Sega's pastel shooter: fly Opa-Opa, shop for weapons, and break the enemy bases.
SNK's time-warp brawler: modern-day fighters against ghost samurai, on the Neo Geo.
Atari's four-player dungeon crawl: Warrior, Valkyrie, Wizard and Elf, and the Elf needs food badly.
Namco's spy run and gun: duck behind doors, count your bullets, and take down Geldra.
Sega's science-fantasy role-playing epic, Phantasy Star II to IV on the Genesis.
EA's motorbike racing with fists and chains: win the race, keep the bike, kick the cops off theirs.
Codemasters' tiny-car racing across kitchen tables and bathtubs, best with friends on one screen.
Naughty Dog's PlayStation platformer trilogy: spin, jump and break every crate.
Goku and the Z fighters in Banpresto's arcade Dragon Ball Z games and Hyper Dimension on the SNES.
Namco's underground pump-and-pop maze game and its island-cracking sequel.
Nintendo's boxing from behind the boxer: read the tells, dodge, then hit back.
SNK's giant-monster wrestling: stomp the city, then pin your rival in it.
